checks.claim: Stars are born in nebulae (molecular clouds of gas and dust), in their coldest, densest clumps; dense cores are about 10 K (about -263 C), clouds 10-20 K, so 'about 260 degrees below zero Celsius' is right
Key: cold gas pushes back too weakly to resist gravity (Jeans instability: collapse when gravity beats thermal energy; colder gas, lower sound speed, lower Jeans mass)
Wrong: gas gains extra gravity as it cools (gravity depends on mass, not temperature)
Wrong: cold gas catches fire more easily (nothing burns; a protostar heats by contraction)
Wrong: cold gas is drawn in by the gravity of nearby stars (collapse is the clump's own self-gravity; triggering by shocks is a different thing and not gravity of nearby stars)
Context: the collapsing clump becomes a protostar that heats as it shrinks
A 16-solar-mass (B0) star lives about 10 million years on the main sequence; a 1-solar-mass star about 10 billion (OpenStax Table 22.1)
Key: its hotter core burns its fuel far faster (fusion rate depends very strongly on core temperature; core temperature set by mass, weight of overlying layers)
Context arithmetic: 16 times the fuel, a thousandth the life, so burned thousands of times faster (about 16,000x; L ~ M^3.5 gives ~16,000 Suns)

Wrong: cooler core (it is hotter); gravity crushes it before fuel runs out (core collapse comes only after fusion fuel is spent); fuel of another kind (both burn core hydrogen on the main sequence; the CNO cycle is a different route, not a different fuel)
William Herschel coined 'planetary nebula' (1785) because they looked like planetary discs in early telescopes; the name is a misnomer
The Ring Nebula (M57) is a planetary nebula with a hot white dwarf (about 125,000 K) at its centre, cast off by a Sun-like star
Key: gas cast off by a dying Sun-like star (planetary nebulae come from stars of about 0.8 or 1 to 8 Suns)
Wrong: planets forming (protoplanetary disc), stars being born (star-forming region), massive-star explosion (supernova remnant): none is a planetary nebula

Context: red giant, outer layers cast off, white dwarf about Earth's size left; the Sun will end this way (red giant in about 5 billion years, envelope ejected as a planetary nebula, white dwarf of about half its mass); massive stars end in supernovae

Betelgeuse: red supergiant at Orion's right shoulder, reddish; Rigel: blue supergiant at the hunter's left foot, blue-white; both far larger and brighter than the Sun (about 95,000-200,000 and 120,000 Suns); both among Orion's two brightest
Key: Rigel's surface (about 12,100 K) is far hotter than Betelgeuse's (about 3,500 K); Sun 5,772 K, so 'the Sun's 5,800' is fair

Wrong: Rigel far closer (Rigel about 848-863 ly; Betelgeuse 400-724 ly by every estimate, so Betelgeuse is nearer); Rigel far larger (Rigel about 78-79 solar radii, Betelgeuse 640-1,200); Betelgeuse hotter (reverse)
Context: red-means-hot misconception from the red of a fire is documented among students

Ejnar Hertzsprung, Danish, published the first colour-magnitude diagrams in 1911 (Pleiades and Hyades, at Potsdam); Russell, at Princeton, independently in 1913; 'worked separately between 1911 and 1913'
Russell at Princeton (professor 1911, observatory director 1912); plotted absolute magnitude against spectral type
'True brightness against surface temperature' as a simplification of magnitude (cluster stars at one distance, or absolute) against colour or spectral type
Key: the main sequence runs from hot, bright stars to cool, dim ones; about 90 percent of stars; position set primarily by mass
Wrong: hot-dim to cool-bright (that is roughly the white-dwarf-to-giant direction, not the band); equal brightness; equal temperature: all false
Context: the chart also showed bright, cool giants above the band and faint white dwarfs below it
checks.note: Acceptable: Russell's diagram showed a sparse group (Linda Hall and a Cambridge IAU paper say a lone dot, 40 Eridani B) of faint stars below the band, later identified as white dwarfs; the name and the class came later. Optional tightening: 'and faint stars below it, later known as white dwarfs'.

checks.claim: Context: Russell first read the diagram as an age sequence (stars start large, cool and red, contract and heat, then cool down the main sequence); nuclear energy 'brought about drastic revisions in Russell's scheme'
Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky; Sirius B first seen by Alvan Graham Clark on 31 January 1862
Sirius B surface about 25,000-25,200 K, over four times the Sun's 5,772 K (about 4.3x)

'Less than a tenth as much light': luminosity 0.024 L_sun (Grokipedia, bolometric) and 0.02448 L_sun (current Wikipedia infobox; older figure 0.056); its visible light alone is far less still. 'Less than a tenth' is safe under every figure; do not state a single number
Key: about Earth-sized (radius about 0.008 solar radii, about 5,600-5,800 km; 'comparable in size to Earth'), with about the Sun's mass (0.98-1.02)
Wrong: gravity traps most of its light (no: it is not a black hole); only patches hot; newborn star (it is a white dwarf remnant): all false
Context: white dwarfs sit below the main sequence on the hot (left) side of the H-R diagram
A white dwarf burns no fuel and is held up by electron degeneracy pressure (tightly squeezed electrons)
Chandrasekhar (born 19 October 1910) worked out the limit on his 1930 voyage from India to England (left Bombay 31 July, London 19 August), aged 19, by adding special relativity
Key as an answer to 'What did he find?' on the 1930 voyage: at most about 1.4 times the Sun's mass
checks.note: The modern limit is about 1.4 (1.44) Suns, and Wikipedia and Israel (quoted in Physics Today) tie the limit's derivation to the voyage. But MacTutor (St Andrews) and Grokipedia say his first figure (the 1931 paper) was about 0.91 Suns, because stars' mean molecular weight was then taken as 2.5; when it was revised to 2.0 his result became 1.44. A historian could object that he did not find '1.4' on the ship. Cheap fix, key unchanged: end the stem 'What is that limit, as we figure it today?' and add to the context 'His own first figure was about 0.91 Suns, because stars' make-up was then misjudged; with the make-up we now know, his sums give about 1.4.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices 14, 140 and 'any mass at all' are false for the white-dwarf limit (any mass is what the older non-relativistic theory and Eddington implied)
Context: relativistic electrons' push cannot keep up with gravity; above the limit a dead core collapses to a neutron star or black hole; Fowler's non-relativistic sums (1926) set no ceiling
Context: Eddington held that electron pressure could hold up any mass (he proposed the non-relativistic pressure law hold at all densities, and that all stars end as white dwarfs 'without a limit')
January 1935 (11 January), Royal Astronomical Society, London: Chandrasekhar presented; Eddington spoke right after and attacked the limit
Eddington's words, given in indirect speech (no quotation marks): 'I think there should be a law of Nature to prevent a star from behaving in this absurd way!'
'Britain's leading astrophysicist' (Wikipedia: 'the established British astrophysicist')
Key: what Eddington found absurd was collapse beyond the limit with nothing to halt it (Grokipedia: he dismissed 'stellar collapse beyond the mass limit as absurd')
Wrong: an Earth-sized, Sun-heavy dead star (Eddington accepted white dwarfs and held that all stars end as them); a blast; swelling into a giant: none was his objection
Context: Bohr and Pauli agreed with Chandrasekhar but, 'given Eddington's standing', would not say so in public
checks.note: That they agreed and stayed out of it in public is solid. The motive is not agreed: Wikipedia says 'owing to Eddington's status'; MacTutor says Bohr and Pauli declined to join the discussion 'saying they were too busy'; Grokipedia says they advised against a direct confrontation. Fix: drop the motive, e.g. 'Niels Bohr and Wolfgang Pauli agreed with Chandrasekhar but kept out of the quarrel in public'.

checks.claim: Context: Eddington never recanted (died 1944); white dwarfs weighed fall below the limit; neutron stars and black holes found; Chandrasekhar shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics (with William A. Fowler)
Song dynasty astronomers recorded a guest star on 4 July 1054 (summer); visible in daylight about 23 days and at night about 653 days (nearly two years), fading by April 1056
The Crab Nebula is its remnant, near that place in the sky (the Chinese record's direction from Zeta Tauri is debated; 'near that place' is safe); still expanding at up to about 1,500 km/s
Key: a massive star exploding as a supernova (Type II core-collapse; progenitor about 8-10 Suns)
Wrong: Sun-like star casting off layers (planetary nebula); new star lighting up; comet: all false for SN 1054

Context: about 6,500 light-years (Grokipedia SN 1054; Crab Nebula page also gives 6,200); Crab Pulsar a neutron star about 20 km across (Grokipedia and Wikipedia Crab Pulsar: 'roughly 20 kilometres in diameter')
Context: a Sun-like star ends with no supernova
Jocelyn Bell, a PhD student at Cambridge under Antony Hewish, helped build the radio array, which 'took two years to build' (her own account)
Quotation 'bit of scruff': her own words, 'a bit of "scruff" on the records' (Little Green Men, White Dwarfs or Pulsars?, 1977 speech)
Pulses every 1.337 seconds (resolved 28 November 1967); nickname LGM-1, 'Little Green Men 1', given by Bell and Hewish
Key: a fast-spinning neutron star (a pulsar is a rotating neutron star beaming radiation like a lighthouse; PSR B1919+21 is one)
Wrong: pulsing white dwarf (proposed in the 1968 paper, ruled out); binary orbit; young flaring star: none is the source

Context: the 1968 Nature paper suggested 'oscillations of white dwarf or neutron stars'; the Crab Pulsar (1968, in the SN 1054 remnant, about 30 turns a second, 33 ms) was too fast for other models and proved pulsars are rotating neutron stars
Context: neutron star more massive than the Sun (typically about 1.4 Suns) yet about 20 km across
Context: the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Hewish (cited for his 'decisive role in the discovery of pulsars') and Martin Ryle (aperture synthesis); Bell was left out

unit_notes: 8 ok, 0 error, 2 uncertain. Both uncertain items are history-of-science precision, not astronomy, and each has a one-line fix that keeps the key. 30ddd9467d: on the 1930 voyage Chandrasekhar's own first figure was about 0.91 Suns (mean molecular weight then taken as 2.5); the 1.44 came after the composition was revised; reword the stem to ask the limit 'as we figure it today' and say so in the context. 69874dc35d: Bohr and Pauli stayed out in public, but the motive ('given Eddington's standing', Wikipedia) is not agreed (MacTutor: they said they were too busy); drop the motive. Sirius B luminosity: Grokipedia 0.024, current Wikipedia infobox 0.0245 (the 0.056 is an older figure); 'less than a tenth' is safe under all, and its visible light alone is far less. Optional in 9eef39910b: Russell's diagram showed one or a few faint stars below the band, later known as white dwarfs; 'faint white dwarfs below it' is acceptable but could say 'faint stars below it, later known as white dwarfs'.
